title: Westpac eyes Wall Street-style loan carve-up to work balance sheet
full_text:
Westpac is preparing to dramatically increase how much of its loan book is sliced up and backed by private credit giants and superannuation funds, bringing in a former Goldman Sachs banker to deploy a Wall Street-inspired approach in the hope of finding investors and freeing up capital.
The strategy to divide parts of the mortgage and business loan book goes further than its rivals and comes amid strong demand from the likes of Blackstone, KKR, PIMCO and other global credit funds for exposure to Australian lending.
Westpac is attempting to add sophistication its loan book management. Edwina Pickles
Blackstone has already acquired HSBC’s $36 billion mortgage book, while KKR and PIMCO acquired a $15.4 billion collection of mortgages from Westpac’s now-closed subsidiary RAMS.
Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller has brought in former Goldman Sachs partner Rob Taylor to oversee the strategy, which extends existing efforts to securitise and sell home loans to other parts of the bank.
Taylor will work with Nell Hutton, another former Goldman Sachs partner who now runs Westpac’s institutional banking division, to find opportunities for investors, freeing up the balance sheet for other uses.
Miller – also a former Goldman Sachs partner – told his senior executives last week that Taylor would “help us think more sharply about how we optimise debt products, improve capital efficiency and strengthen the return on client relationships across the group”.
Westpac’s deepening ties with private credit funds come as the loosely regulated sector falls under intense scrutiny amid the collapse of Bathla, a Sydney property developer that failed owing more than $3.3 billion, almost entirely to non-bank lenders.
The corporate regulator is also monitoring how assets and loans are valued by these credit providers.
But Hutton said Westpac had a long history of originating and underwriting credit, which the bank would use “to distribute more risk into domestic and global asset managers” who remain keen for deals despite the volatility.
Banks already package up home loans into so-called residential mortgage-backed securities, better known as RMBS, and sell them to investors. In the United States and Europe, however, major banks are using increasingly sophisticated strategies to offload debts.
Last year, for instance, some of the biggest Wall Street banks – Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and five others – sold the debt they lent to Tesla chief executive Elon Musk to buy Twitter, now known as X, to investors including PIMCO for around US98¢ and US97¢ in the dollar. The seven banks had originally lent Musk around $US13 billion ($18 billion).
Analysts said Westpac’s strategy was cutting-edge for an Australian lender, and appeared to mimic some of the moves made by US and European peers, who had first adopted these structures after the global financial crisis.
“There appears to be strong interest from global alternative managers for Aussie credit risk,” said UBS analyst John Storey. “Institutional banking margins are low, and the ability to originate and distribute risk – thereby increasing balance sheet velocity – is an important part of improving returns. This is similar to what you would see in the US and Europe.”
Taylor will build new securitisation vehicles, consider secondary loan sales, portfolio sales, and what Westpac describes as “funded loan distribution” – or the sale of some of the risk the bank takes on to outside investors.
Investors should welcome plan
Westpac’s institutional loan book of more than $125 billion grew by 23 per cent in the last half year, funding a broad range of sectors including data centres, renewable energy projects, the defence industry and healthcare.
“There are a lot of large global asset managers and domestic super funds who, if you look at the credit exposure Westpac originates, would love to own some of that,” Hutton said. “Where we have clients who need a lot of financing, this enables us to lend them more money because we have an investor standing behind us who wants to take some of the credit risk.”
National Australia Bank is also planning closer relationships with global credit investors, launching an initiative to tap institutional asset managers as part of its $30 billion plan for financing of new housing supply.
Brian Johnson, an analyst at MST Marquee, said Westpac’s plan would be well received by investors if it reduced risk while increasing returns. “I would hate to think they’re just doing this for regulatory capital arbitrage. But if they are actually reducing the risk over the cycle for ordinary shareholders – it is a good thing.”
One reason that US and European banks moved more quickly to implement these strategies is that rules introduced after the global financial crisis penalised them for holding less liquid assets on their balance sheet. This forced the lenders to become more creative to free up capital.
In contrast, Australian banks are largely funded with customer deposits, and books of mostly variable-rate mortgages have less interest rate risk.
“We might cap out on credit appetite, due to concentration limits or broader risk appetite,” Hutton said. “We don’t have, and no bank in the world has, unlimited capital and funding. And so for us, giving our clients more financing and being able to distribute risk gives us more capacity.”
Before joining Westpac last week, Taylor was a Goldman Sachs partner for 3½ years, based in Hong Kong, where he was co-head of its global currencies and emerging markets team in the region and also ran credit trading, mortgages, real estate and structured financing.
He was previously head of global credit trading and financing at Deutsche Bank, where he worked with Miller, who was chief executive before joining Westpac. Other senior Westpac staff are also Goldman Sachs alumni, including Paul Fowler, who now runs the business banking division.
Taylor is one of several significant hires for Westpac in recent weeks.
Rebecca James has joined from ASB Bank in New Zealand. She is the former chief executive of Humm, which tried to build a buy now, pay later product to compete with Zip and Afterpay.
The bank also hired Caroline Bowler, the former chief executive of BTC Markets, as head of digital assets.
